7179: How does the death (and life and resurrection) of Jesus save?
7180:
All Christians confess that 'Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures' (1 Cor 15:3), but the creeds never defined how the cross saves. The New Testament itself uses many images: ransom and redemption from the slave market, sacrifice and blood from the temple, victory over powers from the battlefield, reconciliation from personal relationships, justification from the law court, healing and new birth from the body. Theologians have built 'models' or 'theories' around one or more of these images.

Nine models are compared here, roughly in the order they were articulated: recapitulation (Irenaeus), ransom (Origen and Gregory of Nyssa), Christus Victor (named by Gustaf Aulén in 1931 as the 'classic' view), satisfaction (Anselm, 1098), moral influence (Abelard), penal substitution (the Reformers and their heirs), governmental (Grotius, 1617), the mimetic or scapegoat theory (René Girard), and the healing or participatory model of Eastern Orthodoxy (Athanasius, theosis).

These are not always rivals. Most traditions combine several models, and many theologians argue that a single picture cannot capture the whole. The real disputes concern which model is foundational, whether God's justice requires punishment, whether God needs to be reconciled to us or only we to God, and whether the cross saves objectively (changing our situation before God) or subjectively (changing us), or both. Each model below includes a 'how salvation works' sequence showing its internal logic.
7182:
Recapitulation (from Greek anakephalaiōsis, 'summing up under a head', Eph 1:10) holds that the Son of God saves humanity by becoming human and living through the whole human story again, this time faithfully. Where Adam disobeyed at a tree, Christ obeys at a tree; where Eve listened to a fallen angel, Mary listened to an angel of God; where Adam yielded to temptation, Christ resists it in the wilderness. By passing through every stage of life, and finally through death itself, Christ becomes the new head of the human race, and those united to him share in his restored humanity.

The model treats the incarnation, life, death and resurrection as a single saving work rather than isolating the cross. Salvation is not merely the cancellation of a debt but the healing and maturing of humanity toward the incorruption and communion with God for which it was created. Irenaeus, who developed the idea against Gnostic teachers who despised the body and the Old Testament, also uses ransom, victory and sacrificial language, so recapitulation is a framework within which other images fit.
7186: From Asia Minor, he claimed to have heard Polycarp, a disciple of John. As bishop in Gaul he wrote against Gnostic systems, insisting on the unity of the Creator and Redeemer and on the salvation of the flesh. His theology of recapitulation pairs Adam with Christ and Eve with Mary.

7201:
Irenaeus wrote Against Heresies around 180 against Valentinian and other Gnostic groups who taught that the material world was the work of a lesser god and that salvation meant escape from the body. Recapitulation answered them by insisting that the same God who made Adam saves Adam, and saves him in the flesh. The idea builds directly on Paul's Adam-Christ typology (Rom 5; 1 Cor 15) and on Eph 1:10.

Aulén later enlisted Irenaeus as the chief representative of the 'classic' Christus Victor type, and Eastern Orthodox theology sees him as a forerunner of theosis. In the modern period, Catholic, Orthodox and some Protestant theologians (including N. T. Wright's emphasis on Jesus as the true Israel) have recovered recapitulation as an integrating frame. As with every model here, most traditions combine it with others: Irenaeus himself speaks of ransom and victory, and Boersma uses recapitulation to hold penal and moral elements together.

7265:
The ransom theory takes literally Jesus' saying that the Son of Man came to give his life 'as a ransom for many' (Mark 10:45). Through sin humanity sold itself into captivity to the devil, who thereby gained a kind of claim over sinners. God, acting justly even toward the unjust, offered Christ as the price of release. The devil accepted the exchange, but in seizing the sinless Son of God he overreached: death could not hold one over whom it had no claim, and by grasping at him the devil lost his hold on everyone else.

Gregory of Nyssa gave this its most famous image: Christ's divinity was hidden under the 'bait' of his human flesh, like a fishhook, so that the devil swallowed the bait and was caught by the hook. Augustine and others used the image of a mousetrap. Proponents stress that God did not owe the devil anything in strict justice; rather, God chose to defeat evil by fair means rather than sheer force, and the 'deception' was the devil's own blindness to divine humility. The ransom theory dominated popular piety for roughly a thousand years and lives on in Christus Victor.
7269: The most prolific scholar of the early church. Commenting on Matt 20:28, he asked to whom the ransom was paid; it could not be God, so it must have been the evil one who held us captive until the soul of Jesus was given, though the devil was deceived in thinking he could keep it.
7272: Younger brother of Basil the Great. His Catechetical Oration explains salvation to catechists; it argues that God, being just, offered the devil a ransom he would accept, and that the deity was hidden under flesh like a hook beneath bait.
7275: Translator of Origen into Latin. His commentary on the creed repeats the fishhook image, carrying the ransom-to-the-devil idea into the Latin West.
7277: Augustine taught that the devil was justly overcome by the justice of Christ rather than by power, and used the image of the cross as a mousetrap baited with Christ's blood. He combined this with sacrificial and mediator language.
7280: In his vast commentary on Job he read Leviathan (Job 41:1) as the devil caught on the hook of Christ's incarnation, transmitting the image to medieval preaching.
